title: Terminal
plain: The terminal is a text window where you type commands and the computer answers with text.
check: Predict: what will the terminal print if you type the command pwd in your project folder?
rubric: Names the folder path as the output
Says pwd only reads and changes nothing
try: Open the terminal pane and type pwd, then press Enter. It prints the path of the current folder.
pitfall: Many people think the terminal can break the computer by typing. Reading commands such as pwd change nothing.

title: File path
plain: A path is the address of a file: the folders to open, in order, and then the file name.
check: Which folder does the path src/pages/home.html sit in, and which file is it?
try: Run ls src (or dir src) and compare each name with the paths in your editor.
pitfall: Windows writes a backslash and macOS writes a slash. Both name the same folders.

title: Version control
plain: Version control records saved states of your files so you can compare them and go back.
check: Your page worked at five and broke at six. What must you have done at five to find the change?
rubric: Says the state must be recorded on purpose
try: Run git --version. It prints one line starting with git version.
pitfall: It does not save every edit by itself; only the states you record.

title: Repository
plain: A repository is a project folder that Git tracks; its history lives in a hidden .git folder.
check: What makes a folder a repository, and how would you see that yourself?
try: Run git status in your project. A repository answers with On branch.
pitfall: A repository is a folder on your computer, not the GitHub website.

title: Commit (save point)
plain: A commit is a save point: a snapshot of the staged files with a short message.
check: Predict: you edit one file and run git commit without staging. What does Git say?
rubric: Says the file must be staged first
try: Run git status, then git log --oneline. Read the newest save point.
pitfall: A commit does not send anything online.

title: Staging area
plain: The staging area is a waiting room: you choose which changes go into the next commit.
check: You changed three files but want one commit for two of them. What do you do?
try: Run git add notes.txt and then git status. The file moves to the staged list.
pitfall: git add does not save a commit.

title: Branch
plain: A branch is a separate line of save points, so you can try an idea without touching the main line.
check: Why would you make a branch before trying a risky change?
rubric: Says the main line stays unchanged
Says you can delete the branch
try: Run git branch to list branches; the star marks the current one.
pitfall: A branch is not a copy of the files on disk.

title: Push
plain: Push sends your save points to a copy of the project on another computer, such as GitHub.
check: After git commit, is your work on GitHub? How do you check?
rubric: Says no, a push is needed
Names git status or the website as the check
try: Run git status. A line says whether you are ahead of the remote.
pitfall: Commit and push are two steps.

title: Permission modes
plain: A permission mode decides which actions Claude Code may do without asking you first.
check: In manual mode, what happens when Claude wants to edit a file?
rubric: Says you can say yes or no
try: Find the mode selector next to the send box and read the current mode.
pitfall: A mode is not a security wall; read what you approve.

title: Variable
plain: A variable is a name that holds a value, so the program can use it later.
check: After let count = 3 and count = count + 1, what does count hold?
rubric: Says the name holds the new value
try: Add console.log(count) after the change and run the file. It prints the value.
pitfall: A variable is not a fixed label; its value can change.

title: HTML page
plain: HTML is the text file that tells the browser what is on the page: headings, text, images.
check: Which line of index.html decides the big title on the page?
try: Open index.html in the browser, change one word in the h1 line and reload.
pitfall: HTML does not make things move; it describes the page.

title: Trade-off
plain: A trade-off means every choice gives something and costs something, so you name both.
check: You pick SQLite instead of a hosted database. What do you gain and what do you give up?
try: Write two lines in your notes: one gain and one cost of your last choice.
pitfall: There is rarely a choice with no cost.
